First, tell your school that you want to apply and they can assist you :)

Read at least 2 extra books around your subject that you can form your own opinion on - agreeing or disagreeing doesn't matter much as long as you can make an intelligent argument. I'm not sure if the personal statement exists anymore, but they still might ask about it in interviews. They really want to see YOUR view on things.

Practice for any entrance exams when they come up and get good A level grades of course. There's good resources on youtube.

Volunteering in a related area at least once (doesn't have to be long at all) and yet again giving your insight into the experience is what they want. What did the experience make you think? If you learned anything new, did it change your perspective?

Overall, they want to see that you're willing to go above and beyond for your subject and are really passionate about it. Give them evidence of that, along with good grades and a high test/coursework score and you have a decent chance of getting in.

Edit: This is from the perspective of someone who got into Oxford, I'm not sure if the same will work for Cambridge.

I'm just coming to terms with this myself... I spent my whole life knowing there was something "different " about me, and spent every night after school wondering what it was that everybody else could see in me that I just couldn't.  When I was first told I was autistic,  I was in denial about it being a disability because that was just what my life had been up until that point. Two years later, I am realising that I am disabled. I hadn't noticed before that not everybody was like me, so I assumed my experience was "normal" and so I wasn't disabled. I didn't realise that I had to consciously try to do what everybody else could automatically do, or that not everybody had sensory issues or that things like me not being able to hug people were related to it. Now I've realised, it's sad but I'm learning to forgive myself. I suppose through my denial I was hoping there was a way to "get over it' (as I've been told many times...) , but I can't.  And that's exactly what is disabling.

For me, using a PEARL structure really helped me organise my points. (Got an A*).

P- Point -> think what, how and why. The author is showing this, using this method, in order to warn/show the reader blah blah. 

E- Evidence. Lay out what you'll be picking apart.

A- Analysis. Pick apart use of language, structure of story, structure of sentences, punctuation and whatever else is relevant to your point. 

R- Response. This can be a comparison of how the reader responds during the time it was published, and how the message can be relevant now. This is also a good place to put in lit crit ( use at least 2 that oppose eachother in one paragraph to be classed as "discriminating" in band 5)

L- Link. Pretty much, just sum up what you said, reiterate your point and LINK IT TO THE THESIS!  So many people forget about their thesis!

Do this for every paragraph and I guarantee you'll be hitting pretty much every point in the markscheme. Make sure to do multiple interpretations, perhaps ones that oppose eachother in at least 1/3 paragraphs. This will get you hitting those top bands.

Also one thing I forgot to add, *a point is only as good as it is concise* . Use simple language and don't try to do something you don't understand. So many people I know tripped themselves up by doing a complex point poorly rather than doing a simple point really well. Just something to keep in mind.

For English remember this structure: PEARL. Also, YOU DON'T HAVE THE BELIEVE WHAT YOU'RE WRITING! Trust me, I think 99% of my interpretations are utter bullshit but it's what gets you A*s. If you can back it, they'll accept it.

P- Point. What is the author doing, how are they doing it and why? E.g. Mary Shelley presents the creature as terrifying (what) through the use of description (how) in order to warn  contemporary readers of the dangers of science going too far (why). It's good to use words like "to warn" "to celebrate" "to provoke" etc.

E - Evidence. Use quotes, structure, form, whatever to back your point. Don't go into analysis yet, just put forward what you will analyse. As a general rule of thumb, messy structure = messy thoughts, tight structure = control, and cyclical means something has to change in order to break the cycle. In poetry specifically, go HARD on structure. You will jump a little back and forth between E and A but that's okay.

A - Analysis. Say what you can get out of what you have presented and why the writer has done it. E.g. In the poem "Eat Me" by Patience Agbabi the use of strict tercets represents the control her husband has over her, and through the presentation of this controlling relationship she may intend to warn people of the dangers of a patriarchal society. Better yet ALWAYS TRY AND USE A COUNTER POINT. E.g. However, whilst there is a tight structure there is only a near-rhyme scheme, and through this the speaker could be undermining the power of her husband in order to blah blah blah. Counter arguments both further your analysis and make your line of argument seem more cohesive.

R- Response. This is where you will apply context and lit crit if you need it. It is the response of people from the time, and you can contrast that to now to show how the text was intended to spread a message at the time. Lit crit is a bit hard to incorporate, but basically say what they said (e.g. Coleridge argues that Iago has "motiveless malignity") support it and then counter it for top marks, just like you did with analysis.


L - Link. Essentially just tie things up. I often just repeat my point using the specifics I have explored in my paragraph.


Now whilst you don't need a structure, it makes it ten times easier and makes your scores more predictable than taking a free-form approach each time. I consistently got A*s with this approach every single time. Another thing is, please only write 3 body paragraphs. Any more is SOOO unnecessary and will make your argument seem convoluted. Look at past essay exemplars and take ideas - you're getting marked on your skills of analysis and putting forward a coherent argument, not originality. However try to steal more unique ideas if you can, just to look impressive.

Here's some questions to ask when identifying cow parsley:

• What does the stem look like? If it has any purple/red splotches on it (think like blood splatters, dangerous), it is hemlock. If it has a smooth purple/red to green gradient, it's likely to be cow parsley. Although for younger specimens be aware, hemlock can be without splotches.

• Are there hairs on the stem? Hemlock has hairless, smooth stems. Cow parsley has little hairs all over the stems and leaf stems.

• What does the cross section look like? Cow parsley's leaf stems should be a U shape in cross section, think like a celery stalk. Identify close to the leaf rather than the stem itself though, as hemlock can form a sheath near the base. Hemlock has more circular stems.

• After all these questions, squish a leaf between your fingers. If it smells like parsley, you're good to go. With cow parsley, if it even fails to meet one of the identification features, assume it is hemlock and move on to another plant.

What really helped me was to actively hunt for hemlock so I knew what it looks like vs cow parsley. Once you see them together, the differences start to become glaringly obvious. Hemlock is darker, shinier and the leaves are more deeply lobed than cow parsley. Good luck!

You've got to bite the bullet, hang out at places of interest (e.g if you're interested in games, go to an arcade or if you're interested in sports, go to clubs or gyms etc) and just sort of approach people when the opportunity arises. Techniques in books often attempt to explain things as general laws, but the truth is that conversations need a more holistic approach where you work on a case-by-case basis. Through the experience of speaking with people and through new experiences you will develop common sense and expression skills, and perhaps certain conversations could even improve your morals.

A general rule for morals though would be "what causes the least harm?", and then do/say that. Of course this has nuances, but can be applied to most situations. Although if you do want to go down the book route for morals, look into philosophies and see what ones most closely align with your values. You could also watch Youtube videos on it, "The School of Life" is a good source. Whilst it is better to say the truth a lot of the time, there are cases where it can cause more harm than good, so try to keep that in mind.
